META — Tier 2 Review (Escalation #24)

Why it moved

Meta reported Q3 2026 results after market close on Oct 21, 2026. Revenue was $64.6B, +26% y/y, beating the ~$63.3B consensus. GAAP EPS came in at $3.83, below most consensus estimates (~$5.46–$5.70), because the quarter absorbed a ~$9.89B one-time legal charge tied to the August 2026 multistate youth-safety settlement; excluding that charge, adjusted EPS was reported around $7.40. I could not independently verify Tier 1's exact cited figures (EPS act 7.25 / est 4.98) against Meta's own release — multiple secondary sources quote different GAAP/adjusted and consensus baselines, so treat the Tier 1 "+45.6%" surprise number as directionally right (a real beat on an adjusted basis) but not precisely confirmed. Capex guidance was narrowed to $135–145B for the year. (CNBC, ppc.land, 247wallst)

Separately, hours before earnings, a New Mexico judge reduced a jury's penalty in a different case — the Cambridge Analytica data-privacy suit — to $25B (down from a theoretical $219.5B maximum), with 15% annual interest and injunctive relief still reserved pending further briefing. Meta is appealing. This is not the "child-safety trial" the position's gate refers to, but it is a fresh, large, dated legal event landing right on the earnings date. (Courthouse News, Washington Post)

I could not get a reliable, confirmed Oct 22/23 closing price — secondary aggregators gave conflicting numbers (some implying a reversal, some implying a drop); this needs direct verification (e.g., a broker quote) before drawing conclusions about the market's reaction.

1A checks

(a) Insiders — distinct count, plan classification. Three distinct insiders sold in the ~5 weeks before earnings: Javier Olivan (COO), Mark Zuckerberg (CEO), Christopher Cox (Chief Product Officer). No insider buying appears anywhere in the data. Olivan's sales are explicitly tied to a 10b5-1 plan adopted Nov 17, 2025, in a recurring weekly cadence (946/629-share lots) — routine, predates the legal news by months. Zuckerberg's Sep 24 sale (27,474 shares, via CZI Holdings/Biohub entities) is flagged on the Form 4 as executed under a Rule 10b5-1(c) plan, consistent with his standing plan entered Jan 31, 2026 per Meta's Q1 10-Q — also routine and pre-dating recent developments. Cox's plan status I could not independently confirm (his sales follow a similar fixed-size, biweekly pattern, suggestive of a plan, but I found no footnote confirming it). Net: this looks like routine, pre-arranged selling, not a discretionary cluster reacting to bad news — but Cox is unconfirmed, so I'm marking this check partial. (SEC — Olivan Form 4s, SEC — Meta 10-Q Q1 2026)

(b) 12-month price/earnings history + peers. Per the stored Finviz snapshot, META sat ~9% below its 52-week high and ~36% above its 52-week low pre-earnings, with Perf Year roughly flat (-0.39%) — not a chronic decline. The pre-earnings softness (down from ~$780 in recent weeks to ~$705-729) coincided with a broad AI-capex sector selloff (headlines Oct 16 show CoreWeave, Dell, and the Nasdaq broadly falling on the same worry), not an idiosyncratic META-specific grind. This supports "macro/sector, not pattern of deterioration" — but I did not run a rigorous multi-quarter EPS-vs-price peer comparison against GOOG/MSFT/AMZN, so I'm marking this check partial.

(c) Fraud/short-seller allegations. I found no short-seller report or forensic-accounting allegation that Meta's reported financials themselves are false. The legal overhang (child-safety settlement, NM privacy penalty) is ordinary litigation/regulatory risk, a different category from an accounting-fraud disqualifier per the framework. Done — no disqualifier triggered.

Index rule

Finviz confirms META is an S&P 500 member (Index field: "NDX, S&P 500"), and it is almost certainly also a top-15 QQQ constituent given its ~$1.8T market cap, though I could not pin its exact current rank this session from a clean, dated source. This is moot for today's purposes: per Appendix A, the index presumption was already overridden at entry (Aug 26, 2026) by a named, dateable catalyst — the child-safety litigation — which is precisely the subject of today's gate review below.

Scores (proposed, refreshed given today's news)

| Asymmetry | Catalyst | Proof | Exit | |---|---|---|---| | 3 | 2 | 4 | 4 |

13/20. Asymmetry is middling — most of the entry-to-now gain (cost $575 → ~$710) is already banked, and a second live legal track (NM privacy case, injunctive relief pending) caps some upside with real tail risk. Catalyst is weak going forward because the dated catalyst that justified entry (the child-safety trial) has already largely fired. Proof (ad revenue growth, engagement, capex discipline) remains strong. Exit stays well-defined (GTC $810; thesis-break = a severe structural remedy or growth breakdown).

Verdict

Applying §6B: the named gate — "child-safety trial resolution; structural-remedy risk (not just fines) is live; Zuckerberg/Mosseri testimony ahead" — has substantially resolved, and on the milder end of the feared range. The Oakland multistate trial (the actual "child-safety trial") settled Aug 26, 2026 for ~$17-18B over 10 years plus conduct remedies (daily time limits, nighttime curfew for minors) — a genuine structural remedy, but a bounded, parent-waivable one, not the business-model-threatening outcome that was the real tail risk. Mosseri testified before the settlement (Aug 25); I could not confirm whether Zuckerberg personally took the stand before the case settled days later — likely moot since it resolved by settlement rather than full verdict.

However, a different, related risk reopened on the exact earnings date: the NM Cambridge Analytica case produced a fresh $25B penalty with injunctive relief still undecided — so "structural-remedy risk (not just fines) is live" remains true for Meta's broader legal exposure, just via a different docket than the one named in the original gate. Combined with my inability to confirm the actual post-earnings price reaction cleanly (per §6B step 2, day-one price action shouldn't be trusted anyway), I don't think this clears to a clean "intact."

Verdict: at_risk. The specific named gate (Oakland child-safety trial) resolved favorably/boundedly, but the broader legal-overhang risk it represented hasn't fully retired — it shifted to a different case with a pending injunctive-relief decision. Recommended check: confirm the actual post-earnings closing price and any post-print analyst target revisions (none found past Sep 28, 2026 in the data provided), and watch for the NM injunctive-relief ruling, before treating the gate as closed.

Why it moved

Liberty Energy (LBRT) reported Q3 2026 results on Oct 21, 2026 (after market close). Revenue was $1.2B (+26% YoY), adjusted net income was $10M ($0.06 adjusted EPS), and GAAP net loss was $39M (-$0.24/share) — the GAAP/adjusted gap is explained by a swing in "other expense" (a $2.7M loss on equity securities fair-value, vs. a large prior-year gain), a non-operating, mark-to-market item, not an operating deterioration (SEC 8-K/10-Q). Tier 1's -166.7% surprise figure is driven by comparing a GAAP-flavored actual (-0.06) against a $0.09 consensus on a tiny EPS base; the company's own adjusted EPS of +$0.06 was a smaller, more ordinary miss against the $0.06–$0.11 pre-report estimate range (financialmodelingprep preview). The stock fell from a pre-print close near $16.70 to roughly $15.38 on Oct 22, then partially recovered to $15.59 (+1.37%) on Oct 23 (stockanalysis.com, marketbeat) — a real but not catastrophic move, consistent with a soft, not broken, print.

1A checks

(a) Insiders — done. Distinct insiders in the Form 4 record: CFO Michael Stock (recurring small sales, 3,333–6,666 shares per transaction, same cadence monthly) is executing a 10b5-1 plan adopted Feb 17, 2026 — confirmed via SEC Form 4 filings (example); this is routine sell-to-cover, not a signal. Director Arjun Murti made two discretionary buys (Feb 17, 2026 and Jul 28, 2026, ~$250K each, $500K total) — one buyer, not a broad buying signal. Chairman Kimble (1 sale, May 5, 2026) and Chief Legal Officer Elliott (1 sale, Feb 6, 2026) each sold once, months before the October decline — not clustered, not discretionary selling tied to the drop. No insider transactions are visible yet covering the post-earnings window.

(b) 12-month history + peers — done. LBRT: Perf Year +39%, but Half-Year -36.9%, Quarter -31.0%, YTD -10.1% (Finviz snapshot) — the stock rallied into a May/June 2026 peak (~$29–33, inferred from insider sale prices) then ground down to ~$15–17 by October. Peer check: Halliburton (diversified, int'l-weighted) is +16.4% YTD, explicitly citing Middle East strength offsetting a North American frac market that "did not recover as strongly as anticipated" and guiding 2027 off zero NA frac recovery (247wallst, shaleexperts). Weatherford (also diversified/int'l) is roughly flat YTD, down ~23% over 6 months. ProPetro (PUMP — a pure-play NA pressure-pumper like LBRT) is -18.7% YTD, down ~24% in the last month alone (chartrow). The pattern: diversified majors are resilient; pure-play NA pressure pumpers (LBRT, PUMP) are both down hard over the same months. That supports sector-wide, not company-specific, weakness — matching the position's own stated gate.

(c) Fraud/short-seller allegations — done, none current. No 2026 short-seller or accounting-fraud report found. The only litigation surfaced is a stale 2020 plaintiffs'-firm notice tied to the 2018 IPO — old, unrelated, and (per the framework's Sep 27 clarification) a bare class-action claim doesn't disqualify on its own regardless.

Index rule

LBRT is Russell 2000-indexed (Finviz "Index: RUT"), market cap ~$2.7B — not a top-15 QQQ name, not an S&P 500 constituent. Index presumption does not apply.

Scores

Not the primary deliverable for a Funnel A review, but as supplementary proposals against the existing thesis: Asymmetry 3 / Catalyst 2 / Proof 2 / Exit 4 = 11/20. Catalyst and proof are soft: the data-center power pivot (SLB/PowerBridge JVs, the Q3-disclosed 1.2GW frontier-AI-lab agreement) is a real, named diversification angle but not yet the thing driving the stock; the core NA-frac leading indicators (pricing, margin) are still weakening in line with the sector. Exit is well-defined (GTC $24/$30, stated gate).

Verdict

Intact. The gate is "sector-wide weakness only, no company-specific break," and the evidence supports that reading: a direct pure-play peer (PUMP) fell by a comparable magnitude over the same window, a diversified major (HAL) explicitly attributes the divergence to international mix rather than NA execution, and the headline EPS miss is amplified by a non-operating mark-to-market item rather than a core operating breakdown. Insider activity shows no discretionary selling clustered around the decline. Per §6B, the day-one drop (-8%) partially reversed the next session, so it should not be read as a final verdict on its own. Watch item: the decline (-37% over 6 months) is steep enough, and Halliburton's 2027 guidance assumes no NA frac recovery, that a continued multi-quarter grind without a differentiating catalyst (e.g., meaningful progress on the data-center power contracts) would start to look less like "patient cyclical trough" and more like dead money against the 24-month rule — worth re-checking at the next earnings print specifically for whether the power/data-center revenue is actually inflecting, which is the one piece of this thesis that is company-specific rather than sector-wide.

CRWV — Tier 2 Review (Funnel A)

Why it moved

CoreWeave fell CRWV stock fell nearly 15% after a sharp move higher in the company's bond yields on 14 October 2026, with the selloff following growing concern over CoreWeave's rising debt burden and the cost of funding its capital intensive AI infrastructure buildout. Specifically, CoreWeave's 9.625% notes due in 2032 were yielding around 14.8%, while its 9.75% notes due in 2031 yielded roughly 14.9%, and the move coincided with news that the company launched an at-the-market equity program for up to 35 million new shares and rolled out plans for a $3.0B private offering of convertible senior notes due 2033 — i.e., fresh equity dilution and fresh debt issuance on the same day. The same day also brought a sector warning: a Gartner report cautioned that 80% of neocloud providers might lose independent viability by 2030 if AI infrastructure spending trends persist, hitting peers too — Nebius dropped 6%, Oracle slips the same day. Management pushed back: management tried to calm things down in an internal memo, calling the market reaction "irrational" and pointing to a sizable deal backlog they say is enough to cover debt obligations. The stock did not bounce back quickly — Finviz's fetch two days later shows another double-digit down day (Price $61.39 vs Prev Close $69.69), consistent with continued, not reversing, pressure through the rest of that week.

1A checks

(a) Insiders — done. Distinct insiders transacting Sept 29–Oct 14, 2026: CEO Intrator, CFO Agrawal, CRO Jones, CSO Venturo, CDO McBee (material dollar amounts), plus four others (McVeety, Goldberg, Baker, Jain) whose "sales" were $262–$438 each — trivial, almost certainly automatic tax-withholding/plan sweeps, not conviction signals, and excluded from the count per the framework's trivial-transaction rule. That leaves 5 distinct insiders selling, zero buying. All of it is classified as planned, not discretionary: the transaction was executed under a pre-arranged Rule 10b5-1 trading plan (Jones, Oct 12–13 sales), and that 10b5-1 plan was established on November 20, 2025, roughly three months after the lockup period ended (Intrator). This activity was primarily executed by co-founders Michael Intrator, Brannin McBee, and Brian Venturo under 10b5-1 trading plans going back to June 2026, so this week's selling is a continuation of a long-standing, scheduled cadence tied to post-IPO lockup/vesting, not a new pattern timed to the decline. No credible discretionary-selling red flag found.

(b) 12-month price/earnings history + peers — done. Per the stored Finviz snapshot, CRWV is down sharply across every window (Month -23.15%, Quarter -15.97%, Half Year -47.46%, Year -56.69%, 52W High -59.18%), so this is not an isolated air-pocket — it's been a grinding, multi-month decline layered with one acute event on Oct 14. However, the Oct 14 trigger itself was sector-wide (Gartner's neocloud warning, peer declines in Nebius/Oracle) rather than a CRWV-only earnings miss, and CRWV's last reported quarter (Aug 11) actually beat on both EPS and sales (EPS/Sales surprise +14.52%/+0.80% per Finviz) — so the proximate cause is financing/leverage repricing, not a results miss.

(c) Short-seller/fraud allegations — partial. Extensive news coverage of the Oct 14–16 selloff (bond-yield spike, Gartner report, debt/dilution concerns) surfaced no short-seller report alleging falsified financials, undisclosed debt, or accounting fraud — the narrative throughout is leverage/financing-cost repricing, a legitimate bear case, not a fraud claim. I was not able to run an additional dedicated search this session due to a tool-use limit, so I can't certify this as exhaustively checked — flagging it as partial rather than done.

Index rule

CRWV is a Nasdaq-100 constituent — CoreWeave, Inc. today announced it has been selected for inclusion to the Nasdaq-100 Index, and is expected to join the index prior to market open on June 22, 2026 — but at a ~$34B market cap (stored Finviz) it is far below the top-15 QQQ names by weight (those are mega-caps in the hundreds of billions to trillions). It is also almost certainly not an S&P 500 member: S&P 500 additions require sustained GAAP profitability, which CRWV (TTM net income -$1.93B) does not have, and no evidence of S&P 500 inclusion turned up. Verdict: neither top-15 QQQ nor S&P 500 — the §3 index presumption (named, dateable catalyst required before scoring) does not apply.

Scores (proposals, 1–5)

  • Asymmetry: 3 — Stock is down ~57% YoY and trades below historical P/S, but the balance sheet (Debt/Eq 10.27, quick ratio 0.46) means a real credit-stress scenario could still produce further equity impairment; upside and downside both look genuinely large.
  • Catalyst: 2 — No single dated event; next earnings date is unconfirmed, and "monitor debt issuance / Q4 margin / rates" is explicitly open-ended in the investor's own record.
  • Proof: 3 — Monitorable, but qualitative: CRWV's own bond yields and future debt-issuance terms are trackable signals, though no hard numeric threshold is defined.
  • Exit: 2 — The stated gate has no defined break condition (what level of bond yield or what Q4 margin number would constitute "broken" is not specified).

Verdict

This is a Funnel A name judged against its own stated gate: "monitor debt issuance, Q4 margin delivery, rates." Two of those three legs were hit directly and verifiably on Oct 14 — a new equity/convertible-debt raise and a sharp spike in CRWV's own bond yields (~15%) — not generic market noise. The third leg (Q4 margin delivery) hasn't been tested yet since the next earnings print hasn't occurred. Per §6B, day-one price action alone isn't the verdict, but here the specific named conditions actually fired, and the stock continued lower through the following days rather than reversing. That is enough to move this from "intact" without yet being "broken" (no default, no confirmed demand collapse, and management disputes the market's read). Insider selling is routine/planned and not a reason to downgrade further.

Verdict: at_risk — the leverage/financing gate is actively being tested; the specific thing to check is whether CRWV's Q3/Q4 print shows contracted-backlog conversion and margin holding up against the now much higher cost of capital.

MRP (Millrose Properties) — Tier 2 Review

Why it moved

Millrose Properties (MRP) is the land-banking REIT spun off from Lennar in Feb 2025 — it buys/holds/develops homesites and sells finished lots back to Lennar and other builders under option contracts. The ~33% drawdown from its 52-week high ($33.49) to $22.50 has two separable components:

  • Sector-wide housing headwind. Mortgage rates have climbed back near 7% in Q3/Q4 2026, pressuring homebuilder stocks broadly; Lennar itself (MRP's largest counterparty) posted what Barron's called its "worst drop since 2024" on Oct 5, 2026, even as Berkshire Hathaway added ~$190M more LEN stock the same week (Barron's, IBD).
  • An idiosyncratic, MRP-specific shock in October. On Oct 2, 2026, Hunterbrook Media published a report finding Millrose had bought 700+ finished Lennar homes across 51 counties/15 states (~$200M+), and was renting them out — allegedly at a loss — despite its 2025 filings stating it would not hold tenants or leases; it noted a filing amendment (signed Aug 27, 2026) that added completed homes/rentals to Millrose's permitted assets. This fed a securities class action, Rubenstein v. Millrose Properties, Inc. (S.D. Fla., filed Oct 9, 2026), naming the company, CEO Darren Richman and CFO Garrett Rosenblum, covering buyers from Feb 7, 2025–Oct 2, 2026. Citizens (JMP) downgraded MRP from Market Outperform to Market Perform on Oct 5, 2026. Several plaintiffs'-firm solicitation releases (Kaplan Fox, DJS Law Group) followed, as is typical after any such filing.

1A checks

(a) Insiders — done. Counting distinct people (not transactions) in the Finviz Form 4 list (Oct 2025–Aug 2026): 7 distinct insiders bought — CEO Darren Richman (two buys, 235,000 shares combined, ~$6.4M, May 11 '26), directors Matthew Gorson (4 buys), Carlos Migoya (2 buys), Patrick Bartels Jr., Kathleen Lynch, COO Robert Nitkin, and General Counsel Rachel Presa (none of these individual buys look trivial under the §1A "ignore a few hundred dollars" test). All listed transactions are open-market Buys — none are sales, and none are flagged as 10b5-1/"sell to cover," so this reads as genuine discretionary conviction buying by a broad set of insiders, not one serial buyer. Important caveat: every buy predates the Oct 2 Hunterbrook report — the latest is Aug 10, 2026. No insider has bought (or sold) since the controversy broke, so this signal is stale relative to the new information.

(b) 12-month price/earnings history + peers — done, with a caveat. MRP is down ~30% over the past year, ~25% YTD, ~22% over the past month — i.e., a grind that accelerated sharply in October. Homebuilder peers also fell this year on rate pressure (DHI reported down modestly YTD as of early Oct per MarketBeat; LEN notably weaker, falling hard off its own 52-week high per multiple reports), so part of the move is sector-wide, not MRP-specific. But the October acceleration (Citizens downgrade, lawsuit, Hunterbrook report) is idiosyncratic and post-dates the broader sector slide — this is a mixed pattern: real macro headwind plus a distinct, unresolved company-specific event, not a pure one-off and not a pure chronic grind either. I could not pull a clean month-by-month peer price chart (only Finviz performance stats and secondary news snapshots), so call this "done" with moderate rather than full confidence.

(c) Short-seller/fraud allegations — partial, and important to classify correctly.
